analysis.one_liner: Requires traveler consent before TSA can scan faces at airport security checkpoints.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with five bipartisan cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since May 2025 with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would sharply limit the government's use of facial recognition at airport security. The TSA could scan a traveler's face for identity verification only with the traveler's clear, affirmative consent, given before each use. Travelers who decline could not be penalized with extra screening, the TSA could not use the technology to track people or run mass surveillance, and it could not share travelers' biometric data with anyone else. It would also have to delete facial images it collected before the law took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, including the millions of people who pass through TSA checkpoints each year. Anyone could decline a face scan and instead show a driver's license or passport, without slower or harsher treatment. The bill also protects travelers' biometric data from being stored longer than needed, shared outside TSA, or used to track people beyond the checkpoint, and requires annual public reporting on how well the technology works and whether it shows bias by race, age, or sex.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Air travelers who decline face scans

how_it_helps.text: TSA could not collect or process a passenger's biometric information except under narrow, consented conditions, and must verify identity with a standard ID document for any passenger who does not opt in.
Consent must be an affirmative act in response to clear notice — standing in a security line or walking through a checkpoint does not count as agreeing to a face scan.

Travelers who opt out are protected from discriminatory treatment, extra screening, or less favorable screening conditions, and the TSA cannot use the technology to track passengers outside the checkpoint or enable wide-scale surveillance.

The TSA could not share biometric information collected through facial recognition with anyone outside the agency, must minimize what it keeps, and must dispose of pre-existing biometric collections that would violate the new rules.

Trusted traveler program members (Global Entry, PreCheck, SENTRI, NEXUS) must be told how their biometric data will be used at enrollment and renewal, and must be given a real option to opt out of face matching at the checkpoint.

The Government Accountability Office must report annually to Congress on the technology's effectiveness, its false match rates, and bias by age, race, ethnicity, and sex, with recommendations to protect privacy and civil rights.

analysis.who_pays: The TSA, which would have to rework checkpoint identity verification to accommodate opt-out lanes and would lose the ability to scan every traveler's face by default. Companies that sell facial recognition and biometric identity systems to the government would lose a large and growing market. Security screening lines could see some friction if many travelers opt out, and the TSA argues facial matching speeds processing.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban facial recognition at checkpoints outright: it lets the TSA keep using it with travelers who consent, so face scanning remains the default experience for anyone who doesn't actively opt out, and people who show up without acceptable ID can still be verified through other biometric means.

It carves out an exception letting the TSA retain travelers' facial images for up to 90 days for 'testing and evaluation' of the software, which privacy advocates could see as a lingering data-collection foothold.

Opt-out identity verification relies on human checking of documents, which the TSA has argued is slower than facial matching; if large numbers of travelers decline scans, checkpoint throughput could suffer, and the bill's annual GAO study is partly designed to measure exactly that tradeoff against security and cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are strong and concrete: no more default face scans, no data sharing outside TSA, no off-checkpoint tracking, and deletion of old biometric collections. The main costs are operational — retooling checkpoints for opt-out lanes and possibly slower processing for people who decline — plus a modest testing exception. On balance the bill gives travelers control over their own faces at a low, measurable cost, though it stops short of an outright ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 8, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it, so it currently goes nowhere.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on May 8, 2025, joined by five cosponsors: Senators Kennedy, Markey, Marshall, Van Hollen, and Daines.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which is the last action on record.

The bill restricts TSA's use of facial recognition to identity verification at the checkpoint, requires notice and affirmative express consent before each use, and lets travelers opt out and show an approved ID instead with no penalty.

It also bars the TSA from sharing biometric data, limits how long it can store it, prohibits using the technology to track passengers or conduct wide-scale surveillance, and orders the TSA to dispose of biometric collections that would violate the new rules.
The bill requires an annual GAO study of the technology's effectiveness, error rates, and bias, disaggregated by age, race, ethnicity, and sex.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the status quo: TSA keeps scanning travelers' faces by default, and biometric screening vendors keep their government market, because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TSA and biometric tech vendors, so far

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Traveler Privacy Protection Act of 2025 to restrict TSA's use of facial recognition at airports.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, one of three Republicans on it.

for.name: Sens. Ed Markey and Chris Van Hollen

against.name: Transportation Security Administration
against.what_they_did: Continues expanding facial recognition at checkpoints nationwide and promotes it as faster and more secure; the bill would curb that program, and the committee has taken no action on the bill since referral.

sides.party_line_note: Three of the bill's five cosponsors are Republicans alongside two Democrats, and no votes or stated opposition appear in the record — the obstacle so far is inaction, not a party fight.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric identity technology vendors
industries.note: Government checkpoint deployments are a growing market for these companies. The bill allows face matching only with a traveler's consent, bans sharing the data outside TSA, limits storage, and orders deletion of existing collections — sharply shrinking what they can sell to the government and whose faces they can scan.

The agency loses its default authority to scan every traveler's face and must build opt-out document verification, which it has argued slows screening. It keeps facial recognition for consenting travelers, including trusted traveler program members.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills die quietly in committee, and this one has seen no action since its May 2025 referral. Its bipartisan sponsorship gives it a path if leadership attaches it to a larger aviation or security reauthorization bill, but as a standalone measure it is unlikely to get floor time on its own.
